opus-5.5.text:
I think positive feedback was really the engine for me, more than any innate love of math at the very beginning. When you're young, you don't sit down and think, "Mathematics is beautiful, I want to devote myself to it." What actually happens is you solve a problem, maybe one that other people found hard, and someone notices. A teacher says, "Oh, that's a nice approach," or you do well in a small competition. That feeling is very addictive, in a good way.

Then it becomes a loop. Because you got that recognition, you want to try harder problems. Because you try harder problems, you get better, and getting better brings more feedback. Over time the source of the feedback shifts. At first it's external: grades, praise, rankings. Later it becomes more internal. The moment where a proof finally clicks, or you see why something has to be true, gives you its own reward, and you no longer need anyone to tell you that you did well.

I also think this applies far beyond math. It's quite similar to how I think about reinforcement learning now. An agent learns what it gets rewarded for, and the design of that reward shapes everything. For a kid, early rewards matter a lot. If the early experience of math is failure and frustration, many people just quit before they ever reach the part where it becomes intrinsically fun. So I was lucky that I got enough small wins early to keep going long enough to discover that I actually enjoyed the thinking itself.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes recognition after solving problems as prompting harder attempts, which build skill and bring further feedback, creating a motivating loop.

fable-5.1.text:
Positive feedback was really the engine for me early on. When I was young, I think I liked math a little, but what made me keep going was that every time I solved a problem a bit faster than expected, or got a question right that others found hard, someone noticed. A teacher would say something, or my classmates would come ask me how I did it. That small recognition made me want to try the next, harder problem, and then the next one.

Looking back, I'd say the loop was: curiosity gets you to try, success gets you noticed, being noticed makes you feel like "this is my thing," and that identity makes you put in more hours. The hours then make you actually good, which brings more feedback. At some point it stops being about the praise and becomes intrinsic, because you've built enough skill that the problems themselves are rewarding. But I don't think I would have crossed that threshold without the external signals in the beginning.

There's a flip side too. When you get a lot of positive feedback, you can start to be afraid of failing, because you don't want to lose that image. In competitions I definitely felt that pressure. So I think the healthiest version is when the feedback is about effort and growth rather than just "you're smart." The people who kept me in mathematics the longest were the ones who got excited about my ideas, not just my scores.

r001.rationale: It describes a repeating cycle in which solving math problems successfully brings recognition, which motivates trying harder problems and investing more hours; that growth then brings more feedback.

astra-6.text:
I think positive feedback can create a cycle. You work on a problem, and at first you don’t know what to do. Then something clicks, and that feeling of understanding is very rewarding. It makes you willing to try the next problem, even if it looks harder.

Encouragement from other people matters too. Sometimes someone recognizing your effort helps you believe you can go further. But I think the strongest feedback eventually comes from mathematics itself—the satisfaction of seeing why something is true. That’s what makes you want to keep exploring.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a repeated cycle: solving a problem brings rewarding understanding, which motivates trying the next, harder problem.

sol-6.1.text: I think positive feedback can create a cycle. You work on a problem, and when you finally understand it, that feeling gives you confidence to try something harder. Encouragement from other people helps, too, especially when you’re struggling and unsure whether you’re making progress. But the most meaningful feedback is often the mathematics itself—that moment when something that seemed confusing suddenly makes sense. It makes you curious about what else you might be able to understand.

r001.rationale: The response describes a reinforcing cycle: understanding a problem builds confidence to try harder problems, and those moments of understanding spur further curiosity.
